metadata.title: Kelly v. South Carolina, 534 U.S. 246 (2002) (No. 00-9280)
metadata.creator: Supreme Court of the United States
metadata.description:
Case name: Kelly v. South Carolina

Opinion filed: 2002-01-09

Docket No.: 00-9280

Citations:
• 151 L. Ed. 2d 670
• 122 S. Ct. 726
• 534 U.S. 246
• 2002 U.S. LEXIS 402

Case holding summaries:
• “Time after time appellate courts have found jury instructions to be insufficiently clear without any record that the jury man- ifested its confusion.”
• "Here, the `narrowing function' was performed by the jury at the guilt phase when it found defendant guilty of three counts of murder under the provision that `the offender has a specific intent to kill or to inflict great bodily harm upon more than one person' "
• "[T]he fact that a defendant is parole ineligible does not prevent the State from arguing that the defendant poses a future danger"
• "evidence of violent behavior in prison can raise a strong implication of `generalized future dangerousness'"
• requiring Simmons instruction when prosecution presented evidence showing defendant's probability of future dangerousness
• "Time after time appellate courts have found jury instructions to be insufficiently clear without any record that the jury manifested its confusion."
• "Time after time appellate courts have found jury instructions to be insufficiently clear without any record that the jury manifested its confusion."
• clarifying that Simmons applies even if an allegation of future dangerousness is made solely as "a logical inference from the evidence"
• “[E]vidence of violent behavior in prison can raise a strong implication of ‘generalized . . . future dangerousness’” (quoting Simmons v. South Carolina, 512 U.S. 154, 171 (1994)
• where the state places a defendant's future dangerousness at issue in seeking the death penalty, the jury must be properly instructed as to the possibility of life without parole
• holding that the state raised the issue of future dangerousness and, under Simmons, the defendant was therefore entitled to a jury instruction regarding the defendant's eligibility for parole, where arguments of counsel were insufficient to inform the jury
• explaining, in the context of Simmons, that "[a] jury hearing evidence of defendant's demonstrated propensity for violence reasonably will conclude that he presents a risk of violent behavior[.]"
• noting that the Court had not yet decided this question
• "The only questions in this case are whether the evidence presented and the argument made at [the defendant's] trial placed future dangerousness at issue. The answer to each question is yes and we need go no further than Simmons in our discussion."
• "A trial judge's duty is to give instructions sufficient to explain the law...."
• holding that a capital defendant is entitled to rebut future dangerousness even it is merely implied by the evidence presented at trial, rather than explicitly argued
